To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the accumulation of purine degradation products and the drop of ATP and GTP levels in hyperthermia experiments can be attributed to the enhanced activity of purine nucleoside phosphorylase, adenosine deaminase, adenosinetriphosphatase (ATPase), and xanthine oxidase, and to inhibition of the activity of adenylate kinase.
hyperthermic exposure results in a significant increase in the purine catabolic flux and that the resulting accumulation of purine metabolites is tumor size dependent.

(i) hyperthermia causes an increased degradation of ATP to ADP and AMP; (ii) this degradation is followed by a rapid increase in purine catabolics, which is tumor-size dependent; and (iii) this increase in purine degradation is accompanied by a significant increase in the formation of reactive oxygen intermediates, which may play a key role in the cytotoxic effects of hyperthermia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the biochemical mechanisms involved in heat-induced cytotoxic effects in solid tumors.

the elucidation of the role of purine catarbolites in the antitumoral effect of hyperthermic treatment of solid tumors, and the possible development of a new approach to hyperthermia treatment of tumors.
the role of purine degradation in the antitumour effect of hyperthermic treatment of tumors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hyperthermic treatment of solid tumors is accompanied by increased degradation of ATP to adenosine monophosphate (AMP), which in turn is degraded to hypoxanthine.
the purine degradation pathway may be an important contributor to the cytotoxic effect of hyperthermic therapy.
purine degradation is one of the mechanisms that contribute to heat-induced cytotoxity in solid tumors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the accumulation of purine nucleosides and nucleobases in tumors exposed to hyperthermia may have important implications for both the development of hyperthermia-based therapies and the understanding of hyperthermia-induced cytotoxicity.
the accumulation of purine nucleotides and catabolites during hyperthermia may contribute to the antitumor effects of this treatment.

hyperthermia is an efficient way of inducing ATP degradation, which in turn results in the accumulation of purine nucleotides and nucleosides, and in the formation of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and protons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hyperthermia-induced ATP depletion is accompanied by an increase in the levels and/or formation of purine clobolites.
the accumulation of purine degradation products is not only an indicator of the ATP depletion, but also a potential source of reactive oxygen species that may contribute to heat-induced cell death.
hyperthermia-induced purine catabolic reactions are a major contributor to the development of hyperthermia-induced acidosis.
